plain_english: Can you think of anything more insane than how these supposedly wise people approach their free time? They work themselves to death so they can live better later. They spend their whole lives preparing to live — but waste their actual life doing it. They're always planning for some distant future. But putting things off is the biggest waste of life there is. It steals day after day from us. It sacrifices the present by promising something better tomorrow. Nothing blocks real living like waiting — losing today while depending on tomorrow. You're betting on what fortune controls, while letting go of what you actually control. Where are you looking? What are you reaching for? Everything in the future is uncertain. Live right now.
original_excerpt: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom? They live laboriously, in order that they may live better; they fit themselves out for life at the expense of life itself, and cast their thoughts a long way forwards: yet postponement is the greatest waste of life: it wrings day after day from us, and takes away the present by promising something hereafter: there is no such obstacle to true living as waiting, which loses to-day while it is depending on the morrow. You dispose of that which is in the hand of Fortune, and you let go that which is in your own. Whither are you looking, whither are you stretching forward? everything future is uncertain: live now straightway.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 9

plain_english: Listen to what the greatest poet tells you. He sings these healthy words as if heaven itself inspired him: 'The best day of our wretched lives is the first one to slip away.' Why do you hesitate? he asks. Why do you hold back? If you don't grab it, it will escape. Even if you do grab it, it will still fly away. So we need to use our time as quickly as time itself moves. We should drink from it like we're drinking from a rushing river that won't flow forever. The poet also brilliantly mocks our endless fantasies. Notice he doesn't say 'the first age' but 'the first day.' Why are you lazy and slow when time flies so fast? Why do you picture long months and years stretching ahead — as many as your greedy heart wants? He's talking to you about one day. And it's racing by.
original_excerpt: See how the greatest of bards cries to you and sings in wholesome verse as though inspired with celestial fire:— "The best of wretched mortals' days is that Which is the first to fly." Why do you hesitate, says he, why do you stand back? unless you seize it it will have fled: and even if you do seize it, it will still fly. Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running. The poet, too, admirably satirizes our boundless thoughts, when he says, not "the first age," but "the first day." Why are you careless and slow while time is flying so fast, and why do you spread out before yourself a vision of long months and years, as many as your greediness requires? he talks with you about one day, and that a fast-fleeting one.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 9

plain_english: There's no doubt about it: the best days slip away first for miserable people — that is, for busy people. Their minds are still childish when old age catches up with them. They reach it unprepared, with no weapons to fight back. They never looked ahead. They stumble into old age all at once. They never noticed it sneaking up on them day by day. Just as conversation, reading, or deep thinking can fool travelers — suddenly they find themselves at their destination before they realized they were getting close — so it is with this fast, never-stopping journey of life. We travel at the same speed whether we're asleep or awake. But busy people never notice they're moving until they reach the end.
original_excerpt: There can, then, be no doubt that the best days are those which fly first for wretched, that is, for busy mortals, whose minds are still in their childhood when old age comes upon them, and they reach it unprepared and without arms to combat it. They have never looked forward: they have all of a sudden stumbled upon old age: they never noticed that it was stealing upon them day by day. As conversation, or reading, or deep thought deceives travellers, and they find themselves at their journey's end before they knew that it was drawing near, so in this fast and never-ceasing journey of life, which we make at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake, busy people never notice that they are moving till they are at the end of it.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 9
